extracted.intended_audience: scientists and researchers (physics, engineering, zoology, fisheries), readers of Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Extract evaluation criteria and standards implied or stated in historical Nature pieces for judging scientific theories, experiments, and empirical studies (physics, engineering experiments, and fisheries research). Emphasizes methodological, evidential, and presentation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of mathematical theory and practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material by separating the mathematical treatment of a subject from its practical applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: increase utility to different classes of readers—some interested chiefly in theory, others in practical details. (R. T. Glazebrook: stated plan to separate treatments to serve diverse readers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise terminology and acknowledge distinct phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accurate technical terms (e.g., distinguish 'shearing' from 'cutting' where appropriate) and recognize different aspects of an action rather than blanket labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing tools or processes, identify the mechanical mode (shearing vs cutting) and relate terminology choice to the phenomena under study; be consistent with the title/content you present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of elastic-strain analysis for tool performance
rubrics_metrics.description: When analysing tools (e.g., tool steel), emphasise stresses and strains produced within the elastic range because tool usefulness depends on avoiding permanent deformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include distribution of stress in the tool under elastic conditions; relate elastic-range results to manufacturers' concerns about permanent deformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report both quantitative (within known laws) and qualitative (plastic-region) effects and acknowledge limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In experimental reports (e.g., photo-elastic studies), present quantitative results where laws permit and qualitative observations where current knowledge cannot fully interpret effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore observed effects even if interpretation is incomplete (examples: discontinuous vs continuous action, curling vs straight shavings); explicitly state where theory/knowledge is insufficient to explain observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intensities as well as frequencies in spectral theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful theory of spectral lines must explain not only the sequence of radiation frequencies but also the relative intensities of successive lines in a series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quantum-theoretic insight that transitions between states with smaller quantum numbers are more probable, and check that assignments correspond to observed line intensities (e.g., an intense line should not be assigned a combination implying low transition probability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overfitting / excessive parameter freedom in explanatory formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt combination formulas or models that permit arbitrary choice of many parameters such that a large number of lines can be fitted by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a formula allows free choice of several numbers (e.g., four or six), demonstrate that matches are not fortuitous; prefer parsimonious models with constrained parameter choices to avoid numerology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical assessment of coincidences versus chance
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed matches occur in regions of high line density, assess whether agreements are expected by chance rather than indicating physical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey density of frequencies and test whether apparent coincidences are more numerous or accurate than would be expected randomly; do not treat dense-region matches as strong evidence without statistical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit early series members without resorting to large quantum numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid spectral assignment should be able to fit the early, prominent members of a line series using reasonable (not excessively large) quantum numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If good fits for early (strong, widely separated) lines require very large quantum numbers, suspect fortuitous fitting rather than physical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and regularity of parameter assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Best-fit quantum numbers or parameters should be unique (or narrowly determined) and show regular sequences when arranged by frequency or intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple distinct parameter combinations fitting the same line indicate weakness in the model; lack of regular patterns (and absence of characteristic differences for singlet vs doublet series) undermines physical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physically appropriate constants and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose constants (e.g., Rydberg constant) appropriate to the physical system under study (neutral atom vs ionised species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the Rydberg constant appropriate only to ionised species blindly to neutral atoms if electron-nucleus coupling differs; justify choice of constants by physical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize increased parameter problems for more complex atoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Be extra cautious applying combination principles to atoms with more degrees of freedom (e.g., lithium when six numbers may be permitted), since parameter proliferation increases chance fits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly evaluate how added degrees of freedom affect the interpretability and statistical significance of matches; prefer explanations with constrained degrees of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two complementary methods to test identity of atomic weights (isotope demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish whether atoms of an element are identical in weight either by direct comparison of individual atoms or by showing chemically pure samples from different sources have different atomic weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct comparisons (e.g., positive-ray/mass-spectrograph analysis) provide definitive evidence; demonstrating differing atomic weights from different sources (e.g., radioactive leads) is an alternative indirect route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select analytical methods appropriate to the physical scale and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose analytical/detection techniques that are capable at the scale of interest (e.g., chemical balance, micro-balance, spectrum analysis, ordinary and ultra microscopes, mass-spectrograph, radioactivity detection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table of limiting analytical methods versus cube/particle size as guidance to determine which methods are feasible for detecting or measuring structures at various scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision requirements for isotopic determination (mass-spectrograph use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments (mass-spectrograph) with sufficient accuracy (order of one-tenth percent) to resolve isotopic constituents reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated examples: mass-spectrograph established neon as 20 and 22, chlorine as 35 and 37; specify instrument accuracy and calibrations when claiming isotopic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ionisation from nuclear transmutation and note energy scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate processes that remove electrons (ionisation) from those that disrupt the nucleus (transmutation), and be explicit about the vastly different energy scales and probabilities involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ionisation is a low-energy, often reversible process; nucleus disruption requires enormous energy and is rare (probability of direct nucleus hit is very small); experimental claims of transmutation should account for these physical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for seasonal and spatial variability in ecological/fisheries studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying fisheries (e.g., herring), take into consideration month-to-month and ground-to-ground variation in catch composition, fish size, reproductive state, and age composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify catches by spawning season (spring vs autumn spawners), reproductive organ development, and sampling location; avoid conclusions drawn from single-season or local samples without broader corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use age-determination and growth-comparison methods (scale ring analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine age and growth patterns by examining scale rings (winter rings), compare growth across offshore and inshore samples to infer movements and recruitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare first-year growth and number of winter rings across samples to infer migration and origin of commercial shoals; relate scale-derived age structure to fishery productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require adequate data before generalizing across regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not generalize fishery conclusions to other waters without sufficient data; acknowledge when further investigation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sample sizes or geographic coverage are limited (e.g., Minch or Irish Sea), explicitly call for additional investigations before definitive statements on age-at-entry or stock structure are made.
